strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing GUI world models for agents generate only textual descriptions of future states, losing visual detail. Proposing a visual GUI world model is a relevant and interesting direction for the agent community.

The Symbolic Text Representation (STR) idea — decoupling graphic generation (diffusion) from text generation (LLM) by replacing text with placeholder boxes — is a sensible and pragmatic solution to the well-known problem that diffusion models cannot reliably render small GUI text.

Evaluation is reasonably multi-faceted: GUI quality metrics, trajectory synthesis, integration into six different App agents (T3A, M3A, AutoDroid, ER, APP-Agent, Mobile-Agent-v2), and an ablation study covering static-text handling and action-instruction conditioning.

The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, including the full prompts, symbol detection procedure, dataset construction from Android Control and AITW, and repeated runs to assess randomness, which supports reproducibility.
Qualitative examples (Figs. 4, 5, 8-10) plus honest failure cases (Fig. 11) illustrate both capability and limitations.
weaknesses: Very small evaluation scale: only 19 Apps, 348 test episodes, and the main results are computed on a randomly sampled 57-episode subset. Headline gains are modest (e.g., ViMo T+1 57.89 vs. IP2P 56.14; step accuracy gains of ~3 points), and no statistical significance testing is provided despite Table 9 showing run-to-run variance, so many reported improvements are likely within noise.

Heavy reliance on LLM-as-judge metrics (sia, sar, trajectory success, action selection) for most quantitative claims. These metrics are noisy and potentially biased, and there is no human evaluation or grounding against real emulator states to validate that LLM judges measure what they claim.

Baseline comparison is incomplete and somewhat unfair. TextDiffuser-2 is used only as motivation in Fig. 2 but is not compared in Table 2; no comparison against strong VLMs (e.g., GPT-4o/Qwen-VL style next-state prediction) or a direct fine-tuned image-editing baseline trained on the same STR-free data. The adapted website world models (Change-text, HTML-text) are weak proxies.

Novelty is moderate: the method is essentially (1) OCR + masking to create placeholder boxes, (2) fine-tuning Stable Diffusion/InstructPix2Pix-style conditioning, and (3) LLM text filling. Each component is a straightforward combination of existing techniques; the 'first visual GUI world model' claim risks overstatement given concurrent work on visual world models for web/UI agents.

Ablation results partially contradict the narrative: in Table 6, preserving static text alone *degrades* performance (T3A 42.81 vs. 43.13; M3A 45.05 vs. 46.01) and only helps when combined with action instructions, yet the paper claims both components 'significantly enhanced' performance.

The pipeline has brittle, hand-engineered steps: colour-based symbol detection with fixed BGR thresholds, heuristic rectangle-ratio filtering, multi-stage LLM prompting to decide unchanged symbols, semantic roles, and text content. Errors in OCR, symbol detection, or any prompt stage propagate, and the paper does not quantify error rates of these intermediate components.

Presentation issues: empty 'Project link:', typos ('Langugae', 'Additioanl', 'overplay', 'VisMo' vs. 'ViMo' inconsistency in Table 4), and a prompt bug in G.8 where the JSON options are '"yes" or "yes"' — small but collectively careless for a top-tier submission.

Limited analysis of when the world model helps or hurts: the System category shows essentially no gain, and there is no analysis of inference cost/latency of the multi-stage pipeline versus simply calling an emulator or a VLM.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: enabling GUI agents to anticipate action outcomes via a world model that predicts future observations in the visual modality, rather than text-only descriptions.

The Symbolic Text Representation (STR) is a sensible and practical decomposition: rendering graphics as pixels while delegating text generation to an LLM sidesteps the well-known difficulty of diffusion models rendering small text.

The evaluation covers multiple angles: GUI quality metrics, trajectory synthesis, integration into two agent families (T3A, M3A), ablations on static text handling and action instruction conditioning, and a randomness check over 3 runs.
The appendix is thorough, including full prompts, dataset construction details, and failure case analysis (Fig. 11), which aids transparency.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scale: the main test evaluation uses only 57 randomly sampled episodes across 19 Apps (test split is only 348 episodes), meaning a single trajectory in Table 3 corresponds to ~1.75% accuracy. The reported gains (e.g., 57.89 vs 56.14 for T+1) are within noise for such a small sample, yet no statistical significance testing is provided.

Evaluation validity concerns: the primary metrics (s_ia, s_ar, trajectory accuracy) rely on LLM-as-judge, and the judge prompts themselves caution that generated screenshots 'may not faithfully represent the real UI', creating potential circularity and bias. The GUI consistency score (DINO similarity) is a coarse proxy for functional correctness.

Novelty is moderate: the core idea (mask text regions, predict layout with a diffusion model, fill text with an LLM) is a relatively straightforward engineering combination of existing components (Stable Diffusion fine-tuning, InstructPix2Pix-style conditioning, PaddleOCR, ChatGPT-4o). The claim of being 'the first visual GUI world model' is likely overstated given concurrent work.

Heavy reliance on handcrafted, brittle pipelines: text symbol detection via BGR colour thresholds and contour ratios, heuristic font sizing and colouring, and multi-stage LLM prompting. These engineering choices limit generalisation and reproducibility; failure cases in Fig. 11 show this fragility.
Dataset is small and narrow: only 19 Apps and ~23.6K images, and AITW action labels were converted to natural-language instructions using ChatGPT-4o, introducing label noise that is not quantified.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the 'Project link' in the abstract is empty, the specific LLM used for the GUI-text predictor and selection model is not clearly stated, and no code or trained model release is confirmed.

Evidence of rushed preparation: multiple typos ('Langugae', 'APP-Agnet', 'Additioanl', 'Subection'), a malformed URL in references, and a clear bug in prompt G.8 where 'ready for action' accepts 'yes' or 'yes', undermining confidence in the evaluation implementation.

Improvements over baselines are modest in absolute terms (e.g., +2.4 and +4.2 step accuracy points for T3A and M3A), and the ablation showing that preserving static text *hurts* when used alone (42.81/45.05 vs 43.13/46.01) is not adequately explained.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: predicting future GUI observations in visual modality addresses a genuine limitation of language-based world models for App agents.

The Symbolic Text Representation (STR) is a simple but sensible idea that sidesteps the notoriously hard problem of rendering small, pixel-accurate text with diffusion models, decoupling layout/graphics prediction from text content generation.

The pipeline is well engineered and reasonably well documented: the appendix provides detailed descriptions of the GUI-text predictor, action selection, data collection, and full prompts, which supports reproducibility.

Evaluation covers both world-model capability (GUI quality and trajectory synthesis) and downstream utility (enhancing six different App agents), with ablations on static-text preservation and action-instruction conditioning, plus a repeated-run variance check (Table 9).

Consistent gains over both language-based (Change-text, HTML-text) and vision-based (IP2P, UI-diffuser, HTML-vision) world model baselines across multiple agent setups (T3A, M3A, APP-Agent, Mobile-Agent-v2).
weaknesses: Evaluation scale is small and possibly fragile: the main experiments use only 57 sampled test episodes across 19 Apps, and several margins (e.g., sgc of 0.7423 vs 0.7414 for IP2P, and step-accuracy gains of ~3 points in Table 5) are within plausible noise; no statistical significance testing is reported.

All key metrics (instructional accuracy, action readiness, trajectory matching) rely on LLM-as-judge, which is a noisy and potentially biased evaluator; no human evaluation or deterministic programmatic checks validate the generated GUIs.

The headline '29.14% relative improvement' is computed against the weakest baseline (UI-diffuser) on the harmonic score; against the strongest baseline (HTML-vision) the gain is only ~5-6%, so the abstract framing is somewhat stronger than the evidence.

The STR extraction and symbol overlay rely on brittle heuristics (OCR plus fixed BGR colour thresholds and contour-ratio rules); the failure cases in Fig. 11 suggest this may limit robustness on real-world UIs.

Limited external validity: training and testing cover only 19 Apps, so generalisation beyond these Apps is untested; the claim of being the 'first visual GUI world model' is also somewhat overstated given closely related work on generative simulators and GUI editing.

The agent-enhancement results conflate the world model's usefulness with the specific selection procedure (a handcrafted two-stage LLM scoring pipeline); an ablation isolating the selection mechanism from the visual prediction quality is missing.
Minor but numerous presentation issues (typos such as 'Langugae', inconsistent 'ViMo'/'VisMo' naming in Table 4, empty project link) suggest the manuscript needed another polish pass.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: existing GUI world models are text-only, and pixel-level generation of small GUI text is unreliable; the paper identifies a genuine gap and addresses it.

The proposed Symbolic Text Representation (STR) is a simple but effective idea: decoupling graphic generation (diffusion) from text content generation (LLM) sidesteps the pixel-level text rendering problem and is well justified both conceptually and empirically (Fig. 1, Fig. 3, ablations in Table 6).

Comprehensive and multi-angle evaluation: automatic metrics, a 70-participant user study, comparison against 6 App agents (Table 2, 9), comparison against multiple world models including adapted language-based ones (Table 3), zero-shot generalisation to unseen Apps (Table 4), online evaluation on AndroidWorld (Table 5), trajectory-synthesis error analysis (Table 10), randomness study (Table 11), and inference-time analysis (Table 12).

Consistent positive results across different agents and metrics (e.g., relative gains of 9.01% on M3A and 14.07% on T3A; 7.76% absolute task completion gain online), plus honest reporting of failure cases (Fig. 6) and error accumulation with roll-out depth (Table 7).

Reproducibility considerations are reasonable: dataset construction from public sources is documented (Table 8), all prompts are included in the appendix, hardware requirements and inference costs are reported.
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on closed-source commercial LLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini) both inside the pipeline (GUI-text predictor, action selection) and in the evaluation itself (LLM-as-judge for instructional accuracy and action readiness). This raises circularity/bias concerns: ViMo's output modality may be systematically favoured by the same family of LLM judges, and results are hard to reproduce exactly as LLM versions evolve.

The contribution is largely an engineering combination of existing techniques (fine-tuned Stable Diffusion with IP2P-style conditioning, OCR-based masking, LLM text infilling); the novel element (STR) is a heuristic representation, and the claim of being the 'first visual GUI world model' is asserted rather than rigorously established against closely related work.

Evaluation scale is modest: only 19 Apps and a randomly sampled 57-episode test subset (justified by a small full-vs-subset comparison in Table 11), and the user study covers 80 samples; DINO-based visual similarity is a coarse proxy for GUI fidelity and is not validated against stronger perceptual or functional metrics.

Gains over the strongest baselines are sometimes small and not uniform: in Table 9, improvements over HTML-vision/IP2P* for APP-Agent and Mobile-Agent-v2 are within ~1-2 points, and ViMo sometimes loses in individual category columns, weakening the claim of consistent superiority.

The action-selection procedure (two-stage scoring with an ad-hoc rule motivated by '70% of tasks have top-2 score gap ≤ 0.1') and the static-text filtering heuristic are engineered shortcuts without sensitivity analysis; the online evaluation improves only one agent configuration (T3A + Gemini-2.0-Flash), limiting the strength of the real-world claim.

The system latency (~2 minutes per decision including three action roll-outs) is substantial relative to baselines like Change-text (~5 seconds), and the practical value of the accuracy-latency trade-off in real deployments is not deeply analysed.

strengths: The problem is well-motivated: existing GUI world models are text-only and lose visual detail, and the paper clearly identifies the difficulty of rendering small text in pixel-space generation.

The Symbolic Text Representation (STR) is a sensible and practical idea: decoupling graphic generation (diffusion) from text generation (LLM) and reducing text content generation to text-localization is a reasonable decomposition.

The evaluation spans several settings (world model quality with automatic metrics and a 70-participant user study, agent decision-making on multiple agents, zero-shot generalization, and online evaluation on AndroidWorld), which is broader than many papers in this space.

The paper includes ablations on static-text handling, action instruction vs. command conditioning, and roll-out iterations, and honestly reports failure cases (Fig. 6) and error accumulation (Table 10).
weaknesses: Heavy circularity in evaluation: GPT-4o is used to construct the dataset (converting action commands to instructions), as the GUI-text predictor, as the evaluator for sia and sar, and as the judge in the trajectory synthesis evaluation. The core claim that generated text is 'accurate' is thus substantially validated by the same model family that produced it. The reported 29.14% improvement may reflect alignment of the pipeline with GPT-4o's biases rather than genuine GUI fidelity.

Very small evaluation scale for the central claims: only 57 randomly sampled episodes across 19 Apps are used for most experiments, and the training set covers just 19 Apps. Generalization claims from 19 Apps are weak; no statistical significance tests are reported for the agent gains (e.g., 49.20 vs. 46.01 on ~63 tasks is within plausible noise, despite the randomness table addressing only the generation side).

Possible confound in the agent experiments: the +ViMo condition appears to also introduce a bespoke two-step action-selection model (confidence scoring plus top-2 comparison, justified by a '70% of tasks' observation). It is unclear whether the baseline agents receive an equivalent selection mechanism, so part of the 9-14% gain may be attributable to selection prompting rather than the world model.

The method is largely a pipeline of off-the-shelf components (fine-tuned Stable Diffusion, PaddleOCR, GPT-4o, color-threshold heuristics) with substantial prompt engineering. The technical novelty is modest beyond the STR representation, and the handcrafted symbol detection (black/white pixel ranges, 0.8 contour ratio) is brittle, as the authors' own limitation section concedes.

The 'first visual GUI world model' claim is overstated and insufficiently grounded; related pixel-space GUI/UI prediction works and concurrent agent world models are discussed only superficially, and no direct comparison to modern text-rendering diffusion models under equivalent fine-tuning is provided (only IP2P*).

Signs of carelessness undermine confidence: the G.8 evaluation prompt literally specifies '"ready for action": "yes" or "yes"', the project link is empty, the abstract/intro conflate LLM terminology, and the ablation in Table 6 contradicts the text (static text alone *decreases* performance for both agents, yet the paper claims both components 'contributed significantly').

Practicality claims are inconsistent: the paper markets ViMo as lightweight and 'plug-and-play', yet Table 12 shows ~2 minutes per request for three action predictions, and the online gains (33.19% to 40.95%) come with no latency or cost analysis in the real-time setting.

Baseline comparisons are uneven: different LLMs are mixed across agents and tables (GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash), making cross-row comparisons in Tables 4 and 5 hard to interpret, and the world-model comparison (Table 3) is run on only one agent in the main text.
Reproducibility is limited: the system depends on proprietary GPT-4o, unpinned model versions, lengthy prompts with stated bugs, and no released code or data at review time.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a genuine gap—existing GUI/web world models predict future observations only as text, losing visual detail needed for App agents—and positions ViMo as the first visual GUI world model.

The Symbolic Text Representation (STR) is an elegant and practical design choice: decoupling graphic generation (diffusion) from text generation (LLM) sidesteps the pixel-level text distortion problem that plagues purely image-based generators, and is well illustrated by Figure 1 and Figure 3.

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple axes: automatic metrics plus a 70-participant user study, comparison against multiple baselines (fine-tuned IP2P*, UI-diffuser, HTML-vision, language-based world models), agent-focused experiments on six App agents, zero-shot generalisation to unseen Apps, online evaluation on AndroidWorld, and ablations on static-text handling, action instruction format, and roll-out iterations.

Good reproducibility practices: detailed dataset construction (Android Control + AITW, 19 Apps, 3,550 episodes), all prompts provided in the appendix, inference-time analysis, a randomness study over repeated runs, and a full-test-split sanity check.

Practical considerations are addressed: lightweight deployment (16GB GPU), plug-and-play API design, and an honest limitations section (Figure 6 failure cases) plus a social impact discussion with safeguards for checkpoint release.

Consistent positive results: gains hold across automatic metrics, human evaluation, and downstream agent step accuracy, and the trajectory synthesis evaluation (Table 10) shows the method degrades more gracefully over multi-step roll-outs than competing world models.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the system is primarily a pipeline of existing components (fine-tuned Stable Diffusion following IP2P-style conditioning, OCR models, GPT-4o prompting, handcrafted colour/boundary detection for symbol extraction). The core intellectual contribution is the STR representation, which is simple; there is little new modelling machinery.

Heavy dependence on closed-source frontier LLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini) for both the GUI-text predictor, the selection model, and even the evaluation metrics (sia, sar are LLM-judged). This raises concerns about reproducibility, cost, and potential evaluation bias favouring LLM-rendered outputs.

Restricted evaluation scope: only 19 Apps and the main test uses 57 randomly sampled episodes; while the full-split and randomness checks in the appendix help, the app diversity is narrow and results may not generalise to the broader Android ecosystem.

Downstream agent gains are modest in absolute terms (e.g., M3A 46.01→50.16 step accuracy; online task success 33.19%→40.95%), and part of the improvement may stem from the two-stage LLM selection procedure (Algorithm 1, Section 3.3) rather than the world model itself; an ablation isolating the selection-pipeline contribution is missing.

Practical deployment claims are undercut by latency: ~2 minutes per request (8s STR generation + 30s text prediction + overhead), which is substantial for 'real-time' interactive agent use despite the paper's framing.

Pipeline brittleness: static/dynamic text separation relies on an LLM, symbol detection uses hard-coded BGR colour thresholds, and the authors themselves acknowledge failure cases where text symbols are not correctly represented (Figure 6); error propagation through OCR → diffusion → LLM stages is not fully quantified.
Project link is empty in the abstract, and no released checkpoint or code is verifiable at review time, weakening reproducibility despite the detailed appendix.
